t: Lesson 3, prompts that survive production.
Your instructor is Patrick Diamitani.
Clever wording isn't the trick. Structure is.
Strong prompts have five parts.
A role. A clear goal.
Constraints like length or tone.
Examples of what good looks like.
And the exact output format you want back.
Put together, it reads like a brief you would hand a smart colleague.
Notice the example points to a file instead of pasting it in.
When the output misses, resist the urge to start over.
Say exactly what's wrong and what to keep.
Starting fresh throws away everything the agent just learned.
For bigger jobs, use a loop.
Ask for a plan. Correct the plan.
Execute it one step at a time.
Then verify the result.
Quick recap. Fixing a plan is cheaper than fixing a product.
Your mission, rewrite one prompt you use every week with all five parts,
then run the plan first loop on it.
That's prompting that holds up.
